Personal Best

Thunderhill Raceway Park sits in Willows, California — a stretch of Northern California that opens up into wide rolling hills and vast open sky. The East Cyclone configuration adds its namesake chicane section to the traditional layout, pushing total distance to 2.866 miles and the corner count past fifteen.

“In the week leading up to the event, I spent several evenings in the simulator learning the layout, studying braking zones, corner sequences, and the overall rhythm of the track.”

The preparation paid dividends almost immediately. Counterclockwise and technical, the East Cyclone rewards patience and commitment — flowing between wide, sweeping sections and tight, slow-speed technical zones. The Cyclone section itself (Turns 5–5A) demands particular care: a compressed series of direction changes that arrive just when momentum tempts you into carrying too much speed.

For a first visit, the strategy was simple: learn the reference points, build trust in the car, and add pace from there. The simulator prep translated remarkably well to the real world.

The Debrief

Track Night in America strikes an impressive balance between accessibility and professionalism. Check-in was smooth, driver’s meetings were organized, and the event maintained a welcoming atmosphere throughout the evening. For anyone looking to make the jump from autocross, sim racing, or spirited backroad driving into their first track-day experience, it provides an approachable entry point without sacrificing structure or safety.

As a first-time Thunderhill participant, I elected to run in the Novice group. Looking back, it was the right choice. It allowed me to learn the track, understand the event procedures, and focus on building confidence without unnecessary pressure.

“That said, I suspect Intermediate may be where I’ll sign up next.”

For the most part, drivers were courteous and aware of passing etiquette. Like any novice group, however, there were a handful of repeat offenders who were slow to provide point-bys. There were moments where traffic became the biggest obstacle to improving lap times. Fortunately, those instances were the exception rather than the rule.

One of the biggest surprises of the evening was the value. Because I participated in the SCCA Starting Line School earlier this season at Crows Landing, my entry fee was only $25 — a recommendation I’d make to anyone starting out. Even at the standard $150 price point, it’s a bargain. The novice group also enjoyed driver’s meetings inside Thunderhill’s air-conditioned clubhouse — a small detail that became increasingly appreciated as the Northern California afternoon warmed up.

From the driver’s seat • Thunderhill East • June 2026

The simulator taught the layout. The real thing taught the commitment. There is a gap between knowing a corner and trusting a corner — and closing that gap, one lap at a time, is what a track day is for.

Verdict

2:22
.26 — Personal Best • First Visit
First VisitPersonal BestNovice GroupTNIAEast CycloneRE-71RZSim Prep#33

The most telling sign of a good track day isn’t the lap time — it’s leaving the pits with a clear sense of what to do next. By that measure, this was a success. The circuit is understood. The baseline is set.

The 2:22.26 represents a solid foundation on a car prepared for SCCA C Street. The RE-71RZ is well-suited to the task — consistent, communicative, and more than capable of supporting real progression at this level. There is real time left on the table, and it sits in the driver’s hands rather than the setup sheet.

Thunderhill’s East Cyclone rewards a driver who can read a rhythm. Come back with more laps in the bank and the Intermediate run group will open up considerably. That’s the plan.

“I left feeling like I understood the track. That mattered more than the lap time.”
